TASKS.text: Write the retrieval pipeline and prompts for an internal support bot.
TASKS.explain: This is core AI engineering work: retrieval, prompting, and wiring it into a production system, exactly Modules 1 and 3's territory.

TASKS.text: Analyze which questions employees ask the support bot most often, to find gaps in the documentation.
TASKS.explain: Analyzing usage data to find a pattern and inform a decision is classic data science, not building the system itself.

TASKS.text: Fine-tune a smaller embedding model because off-the-shelf retrieval isn't accurate enough for this company's jargon.
TASKS.explain: Training/fine-tuning a model is ML engineering territory, the AI engineer would consume the resulting model, not produce it.

TASKS.text: Publish a paper proposing a new attention mechanism that reduces context-window cost.
TASKS.explain: Pushing the boundary of what's technically possible, and publishing it, is research, not applied engineering.

TASKS.text: Keep GPU costs under control and make sure the model-serving cluster survives a traffic spike.
TASKS.explain: Operating and scaling the platform models run on is infrastructure/MLOps work, distinct from building what runs on top of it.

TASKS.text: Add a minimum-relevance threshold so the bot says 'I don't know' instead of guessing from an irrelevant document.
TASKS.explain: Directly building the reliability/quality logic of the AI system, this is Module 3's relevance-threshold concept in a real support-bot context.

ROLE_DETAILS.name: AI Application Engineer
ROLE_DETAILS.build: End-user-facing AI features: chatbots, copilots, AI-powered product surfaces.
ROLE_DETAILS.with: Model APIs, frontend/backend glue, prompt and context management.
ROLE_DETAILS.tools: An LLM SDK, a frontend framework, a vector DB.
ROLE_DETAILS.projects: A support chatbot, an AI writing assistant, a copilot inside an existing app.

ROLE_DETAILS.name: LLM / Generative AI Engineer
ROLE_DETAILS.build: The core LLM-powered logic: prompting systems, RAG pipelines, agent loops.
ROLE_DETAILS.with: Model APIs, embeddings, retrieval, tool/function calling.
ROLE_DETAILS.tools: LLM SDKs, a vector DB, an orchestration framework.
ROLE_DETAILS.projects: A RAG system, a multi-step agent, a structured-extraction pipeline.

ROLE_DETAILS.name: AI/ML Engineer
ROLE_DETAILS.build: Systems that may include model training/fine-tuning alongside LLM integration.
ROLE_DETAILS.with: Training frameworks, evaluation metrics, data pipelines, LLM APIs.
ROLE_DETAILS.tools: PyTorch/TensorFlow, experiment tracking, an LLM SDK.
ROLE_DETAILS.math: Moderate: linear algebra, probability, optimization basics.
ROLE_DETAILS.projects: A fine-tuned classifier, a hybrid ML+LLM pipeline.

ROLE_DETAILS.name: AI Integration Engineer
ROLE_DETAILS.build: Connecting AI capability into existing business systems (CRM, support desk, internal tools).
ROLE_DETAILS.with: APIs, webhooks, auth, existing enterprise systems.
ROLE_DETAILS.prog: Any backend language, strong API/integration skills.
ROLE_DETAILS.tools: REST/GraphQL clients, auth libraries, an LLM SDK.
ROLE_DETAILS.projects: An AI feature wired into a CRM, an automated ticket-triage integration.

ROLE_DETAILS.name: AI Automation Engineer
ROLE_DETAILS.build: Replacing manual, judgment-heavy workflows with AI-assisted automation.
ROLE_DETAILS.with: Workflow tools, APIs, LLMs for the judgment-call steps.
ROLE_DETAILS.tools: Automation platforms, an LLM SDK, a task queue.
ROLE_DETAILS.projects: Automated document processing, an AI-assisted approval workflow.

ROLE_DETAILS.name: AI Platform / Infrastructure Engineer
ROLE_DETAILS.build: The platform other engineers deploy AI systems on top of.
ROLE_DETAILS.with: Model serving, GPU infrastructure, deployment pipelines.
ROLE_DETAILS.prog: Python plus strong systems/infra skills (Go/Rust helpful, not required to start).
ROLE_DETAILS.tools: Kubernetes, Terraform, a metrics/tracing stack, an inference server.
ROLE_DETAILS.math: Minimal to moderate depending on optimization work.
ROLE_DETAILS.projects: A model-serving platform, an internal LLM gateway with cost tracking.

ROLE_DETAILS.name: MLOps-oriented roles
ROLE_DETAILS.build: Operationalizing ML/AI: CI/CD for models, monitoring, reproducibility.
ROLE_DETAILS.with: Experiment tracking, model registries, deployment pipelines.
ROLE_DETAILS.tools: MLflow or similar, CI/CD tooling, containerization.
ROLE_DETAILS.projects: A model deployment pipeline, an automated retraining/monitoring system.

ROLE_DETAILS.name: AI Product Engineer
ROLE_DETAILS.build: Deciding WHAT to build with AI, prototyping features, balancing capability against user value.
ROLE_DETAILS.with: LLM APIs, rapid prototyping tools, user feedback loops.
ROLE_DETAILS.tools: An LLM SDK, prototyping/no-code tools, analytics.
ROLE_DETAILS.projects: A rapid AI feature prototype, an A/B-tested AI product surface.

PRIORITY.why: The dominant language for AI/ML tooling, most SDKs and frameworks ship Python-first.
PRIORITY.now: Enough to write scripts, call APIs, handle JSON.

PRIORITY.why: Version control is non-negotiable for any real software work, AI projects included.
PRIORITY.now: Commit, branch, push, pull, resolve a basic conflict.

PRIORITY.why: Every model API call is an HTTP request returning JSON, this is the literal substrate of the field.
PRIORITY.now: Understand requests, responses, status codes, and JSON structure.
PRIORITY.later: Deepens with auth, webhooks, streaming responses.

PRIORITY.why: Nearly every real AI system persists something: logs, retrieval documents, eval results, idempotency keys.
PRIORITY.later: Query optimization, schema design as systems grow.

PRIORITY.why: Needed if you're building the user-facing side of an AI product, or working in a JS-first stack.
PRIORITY.now: Not required to start if you're Python-first.
PRIORITY.later: Essential for AI application engineers building UIs/copilots.

PRIORITY.why: Most AI infrastructure runs on Linux; comfort with a shell speeds up everything.
PRIORITY.later: Becomes important once you're deploying or debugging in production.

PRIORITY.why: Standard way to package and run AI services consistently across environments.
PRIORITY.later: Matters once you deploy anything real.

PRIORITY.why: Performance-critical inference engines and high-throughput serving infrastructure.
PRIORITY.now: Not needed to start, at all.
PRIORITY.later: Only if you move deep into AI platform/infrastructure work.

ECOSYSTEM.name: Development
ECOSYSTEM.why: The daily tools for writing, versioning, and running code, category is timeless even as specific tools change.
ECOSYSTEM.ex: e.g. VS Code, Git, GitHub, a CLI

ECOSYSTEM.name: Languages
ECOSYSTEM.why: What you actually write the system in, Python dominates AI-specific tooling, JS/TS dominates the application layer.

ECOSYSTEM.name: AI Models / APIs
ECOSYSTEM.why: The actual intelligence your system calls out to, swappable in principle if your code isn't tightly coupled to one vendor.
ECOSYSTEM.ex: e.g. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google/Gemini, Hugging Face, open-source models

ECOSYSTEM.name: Frameworks
ECOSYSTEM.why: Pre-built orchestration for prompting, retrieval, and agent logic, useful, but everything they do is learnable from first principles (which is what this course teaches).
ECOSYSTEM.ex: e.g. LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, and comparable alternatives

ECOSYSTEM.name: Tool connectivity
ECOSYSTEM.why: The wire format a model-facing app uses to discover and call tools exposed by a separate server, standardizes the plumbing, not the validate-then-execute discipline Module 4 teaches, which still applies underneath it either way.
ECOSYSTEM.ex: e.g. MCP (Model Context Protocol), and comparable emerging standards

ECOSYSTEM.name: Data
ECOSYSTEM.why: Where your system's persistent knowledge and state actually live.
ECOSYSTEM.ex: e.g. PostgreSQL, a vector database, Redis for caching

ECOSYSTEM.name: Infrastructure
ECOSYSTEM.why: How your system gets packaged, deployed, and kept running at scale.
ECOSYSTEM.ex: e.g. Docker, a cloud platform, Linux, CI/CD

ECOSYSTEM.name: Evaluation / Observability
ECOSYSTEM.why: How you know whether the system is actually working, and where it's failing, in production.
ECOSYSTEM.ex: e.g. LangSmith, Langfuse, OpenTelemetry-based tracing, an eval framework, monitoring dashboards

PATH_QUESTIONS.q: Do you enjoy building things end-users directly interact with, or the systems underneath that other engineers rely on?
Would you rather wire together existing model APIs, or work on training/fine-tuning models yourself?
Do you prefer customer-facing integration work, or general-purpose reliability engineering?
How much do you enjoy writing deployment/infrastructure tooling versus writing product-facing code?
Do you want a mostly-Python role, or a full-stack role touching both JavaScript and Python?
When something breaks in production, are you more drawn to debugging the model's behavior, or debugging the infrastructure it runs on?

parts.label: 1. Define AI Engineering in your own words
parts.placeholder: In a sentence or two, what is AI Engineering...

parts.label: 2. Which role would primarily handle this task?
parts.question: "Fine-tune a smaller open-source embedding model because off-the-shelf retrieval quality isn't good enough for a niche domain."

options.correctText: Correct. Fine-tuning a model is ML engineering work; the AI engineer would consume the resulting model afterward.

options.reason: AI engineers typically consume already-trained models through an API, training/fine-tuning is ML engineering territory.
Fine-tuning an existing model for a practical need isn't the same as researching a new technique or architecture.

parts.label: 3. Which technologies should a complete beginner prioritize first?
parts.question: Pick the pair that both belong in "need to know now."

options.correctText: Correct. Both are marked 'need to know now', the dominant AI tooling language and the literal substrate every model API call runs on.

options.reason: Both are 'should learn next' or 'specialized', not day-one priorities for a beginner.
Both are specialized/infrastructure-leaning tools, not where a beginner should start.

parts.label: 4. Identify the stages of an AI engineering workflow
parts.question: In the production lifecycle from Lesson 0.2, what comes immediately after "Model / AI API" and before "RAG / Tools / Agents"?

options.correctText: Correct. Backend sits between the raw model/API call and the RAG/tools/agent logic built on top of it.

options.reason: Deployment comes much later in the flow, after Application and Evaluation.
Data comes near the beginning of the flow, before a model is even called.

parts.label: 5. Which skill do you need before going deeper into this course?
parts.question: Modules 1–8 assume comfort with which of these?

options.t: Basic programming fundamentals (variables, functions, loops, dictionaries): no prior Python required
options.correctText: Correct. This course teaches the Python you need as you go, only general programming fundamentals are assumed going in.

options.reason: Infrastructure depth like this is explicitly out of scope for this course, not a prerequisite.
Prior Python isn't required, this course teaches the Python needed for the AI engineering work that follows, from the fundamentals up.

selfCheck.note: This self-check is a reflection tool. It is not a mastery gate, unlike the checkpoints in Modules 1–8, and completing it is optional before continuing.
